desc:
A cloud cost review and savings plan shows where your monthly bill is higher than your workload needs. Ecom Swift LLC reads your billing and resource list, ranks the savings by effort and risk, and applies the safe changes in your own account.

## What is a cloud cost review?

A cloud cost review is a structured look at what you pay for and what you actually use. It compares your invoices with your running servers, databases, storage and network, and flags the gap between the two. The result is a short list of changes, each with an estimated monthly effect and a risk note.

Cloud bills grow in quiet ways. Someone starts a test server and forgets it. A database is sized for a launch that never came. A volume stays attached to nothing after a machine is deleted. Each item is small, and together they become a line on the invoice that nobody can explain.

## Why cloud spend drifts upward

Cloud platforms make it easy to create resources and easy to forget them. Charges continue by the hour whether the resource is busy or idle. Teams change, projects end, and the people who knew why something existed move on.

Pricing itself adds confusion. The same workload can cost very different amounts on different instance families, storage tiers or plan types. Steady workloads can often be covered by commitment discounts, but only if someone checks the usage pattern first. Without a regular review, you pay the default rate for everything.

## How lower spend helps without hurting speed

Cutting cost is not the same as cutting capacity. The aim is to remove waste, not performance. A server that sits mostly idle can often move to a smaller size without anyone noticing. A staging environment that runs overnight can be switched off outside working hours. Old snapshots and logs can follow a retention rule.

Each change has a risk, so we sort them. Deleting an unattached disk is low risk. Resizing a production database needs a test and a quiet time window. You see that ranking before anything is touched, and you decide what goes ahead.

## What a useful cost review covers

- Invoice review by service, region and account, to see where money goes.
- Idle compute, such as servers with almost no CPU or network use.
- Oversized instances and databases that could move to a smaller plan.
- Unattached storage volumes, old snapshots and orphaned IP addresses.
- Forgotten test, demo and former project environments.
- Data transfer and storage tier choices that cost more than needed.
- Commitment or reserved-capacity options for steady workloads.
- Budget alerts so a surprise spike reaches you early.
- Tags by project or team, so each cost has an owner.
- A plain-language summary a non-technical owner can read.

## How we work

We begin with read-only billing access and a resource inventory. We match each cost to a purpose and mark anything we cannot explain, then ask you about it instead of guessing. The savings list that follows names the resource, the proposed change, the expected monthly effect and what could go wrong.

In the larger packages we make the safe changes ourselves, record the before and after state and set up a budget alert. The Premium package extends this across several accounts, adds commitment advice, cost tagging and a monthly report template your team can reuse. Any estimate of savings is an estimate. Actual results depend on your usage, your provider's pricing and how much of the list you choose to apply.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Tag resources by project so costs have owners.
- Set a budget alert at a level that would surprise you.
- Review idle resources before each launch and after each project ends.
- Test any resize on a copy or at a quiet time first.
- Keep a record of every change and its reason.

**Avoid:**
- Deleting a resource you cannot identify.
- Buying long-term commitments before checking usage is steady.
- Shrinking production servers without a rollback plan.
- Judging savings from a single unusual month.
- Treating cost review as a one-time event.

## Who this is for

This service suits a startup founder who sees the cloud bill rise each month with no clear reason. It suits an agency running many client environments in one account. It also suits a team that finished a migration and now wants to right-size what was copied over.

## What we need from you

Send the name of your cloud provider, a few months of invoices or read-only billing access, and a short note on which systems are business critical. We never need your passwords. Access is given as a billing or read-only user in your own account, and you can remove it when we finish.
